headline: First try on snowshoes in Maine
summary: Roosevelt straps on snowshoes for the first time and covers about six miles checking lynx traps with Will Dow. The traps are empty, but he marvels at the snow-heavy evergreens and drops a porcupine from a hemlock with his rifle.

events.detail: Learns to snowshoe on a six-mile circuit of lynx traps
Shoots a porcupine out of a hemlock with his rifle
Notes tracks of lynx, foxes, otters and rabbits

tr_quotes.text: Tried snowshoing for the first time. Went about six miles, making the round of Will Dow's "lucivee' [lynx] traps, which however contained nothing. The woods looked simply perfect, all the evergreens being loaded with snow; I have never seen a grander sight than these northern forests in winter. I got along very well, except in a cedar swamp. We saw many tracks of lucivees, foxes, otters and rabbits; and found a porcupine up in a hemlock. I brought him down quite neatly with the rifle.

uncertain: 'lucivee' is a Maine word for lynx; 'Will Dow' taken as Wilmot Dow.

headline: Bible reading and a winter tramp
summary: A quiet Sunday: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then walks the snowy pine and spruce woods in the afternoon. He finds the cold easy to bear among the trees but harsh in the wind, and notes how little life stirs in the forest.

events.detail: Reads his Bible in the morning
Afternoon snowshoe walk through pine and spruce forest

tr_quotes.text: Read my bible in the morning. In the afternoon took a tramp through the woods; I can not get used to the extreme beauty of the snow covered pine and spruce forests. The cold does not bother me at all in the woods, but if there is any wind it is very disagreeable in the open. I get along very well on snow shoes, but the swamps are very tough work - although perhaps not so bad as in summer. There is very little life in the woods.

headline: Eight hours in the woods with Dow
summary: With Will Dow, Roosevelt hikes to Dyer Brook and then strikes off cross-country through hardwoods and tangled spruce and cedar swamps. Over an eight-hour tramp he logs an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, two gray jays at lunch, and the tracks of hare, lynx and spruce grouse.

events.detail: Long winter hike to Dyer Brook and through the woods
Records an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, whiskey jacks and lynx tracks

tr_quotes.text: Went off on a tramp through the woods with Will Dow. Walked up to Dyer Brook, then a couple of miles along it, and then struck out in the woods. The best walking was on the hard wood grounds; it was fearfully hard work in some of the thick, swampy spruce and cedar thickets, but not as bad as in summer. I saw an arctic woodpecker by a stream and some Halldronian chickadees in a spruce wood, and two whiskey jacks came round us at lunch time; we saw two or three hare tracks, and once the round footprints of a canada lynx, and found where a spruce partridge had passed the night; but in an 8 hour tramp, these were the only traces of life.

uncertain: 'Halldronian chickadees' is as written in the record; TR likely meant Hudsonian chickadees.

headline: A ruffed grouse after a long hunt
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the woods with Bill Sewall. Tracks of a dozen kinds of animals are everywhere, yet they see only chickadees and a woodpecker until they trail a partridge, flush it from a fallen birch and Roosevelt brings it down.

events.detail: Tracks and shoots a ruffed grouse with Sewall
Notes tracks of lynx, mink, weasel, otter and porcupine

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day tramping through the woods with Will Seawall. We saw a good many tracks of lucivees, foxes, rabbits, otters, minks, weasels, squirrels, porcupines + c; but the only living creatures were a couple of chickadees and a woodpecker. Finally we found the footprints of a partridge on some hardwood ground, and following them up roused the bird from under a fallen birch top, and I shot it. The snow shoing [sic] is poor, the snow being wet or heavy, and the weather warmish. 1 ruffed grouse.

uncertain: 'Will Seawall' taken as William Wingate Sewall.

headline: Asthma at night, grouse by day
summary: Another day of snowshoeing with little game to show for it, though Roosevelt is having the time of his life. Asthma keeps him awake at night. After lunch at a logging camp he shoots a partridge from a spruce top and a porcupine; the traps have so far yielded a lynx and a fox.

events.detail: Snowshoes through the woods all day
Asthma disturbs his sleep
Shoots a partridge and a porcupine; traps hold a lynx and a fox

tr_quotes.text: Otherwise I am enjoying myself to the utmost, but the asthma keeps me up a good deal at night.

headline: Thirty miles by pung to a logging camp
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow set out with a box sleigh and a scrawny horse for a logging camp thirty miles off, arriving after dark. It is ten below at the start and the roads are terrible. Along the way he spots a red crossbill, flocks of snow buntings and some unusually tame grosbeaks.

events.detail: Rides a pung sleigh thirty miles to a logging camp
Sees snow buntings, a red crossbill, grosbeaks and mouse tracks

tr_quotes.text: When we started the thermometer was 10° below zero, but I was too well wrapped up to heed the cold

headline: On the trail of a caribou
summary: Through a heavy snowstorm Roosevelt and Dow hunt all day, finally jumping a caribou in thick spruce. He glimpses it at under thirty yards but cannot shoot, and they track it until dark, then spend a cold, hungry night by a big fire with no blankets.

events.detail: Startles a caribou and follows its tracks until dusk
Camps overnight in the snow with little food and no blankets

tr_quotes.text: I caught a glimpse of him as he vanished not thirty yards distant, but had no chance to fire.

headline: Caribou chase ends without a shot
summary: Before sunrise, in subzero cold, the hunters take up the caribou's trail again through swamps, ledges and open cranberry bogs. Roosevelt studies how the animal trots and bounds in snow over three feet deep. By midday they quit and are back at the logging camp at sunset.

events.detail: Follows the caribou until midday, then gives up
Observes how a caribou moves through deep snow

tr_quotes.text: Generally he trotted, coming down not only on his hoofs but on his whole lower legs, the snow being over three feet deep, but in bad ground he made great jumps like a huge rabbit.

headline: Resting among the lumbermen
summary: Worn out from two days after the caribou, Roosevelt rests. His asthma has not troubled him since reaching camp, and he warms to the rough, generous lumbermen, especially one named Charley Brown. Rain followed by frost has coated every tree in ice.

events.detail: Rests at the logging camp after the caribou hunt
Befriends the lumbermen, especially Charley Brown

tr_quotes.text: I like these lumbermen very much, and get on capitally with them - great, rough, hospitable fellows. I am great friends with one in especial, Charley Brown.

headline: A buck, rabbits and a venison feast
summary: Roosevelt and Sewall find a small deer yard. He trips and misses his first shot at the buck, then runs it down over a mile and kills it with his rifle. After an afternoon of rabbit hunting, venison replaces the usual pork and beans. He writes his mother that he has stored up health enough to last into summer.

events.detail: Kills a buck after a mile-long chase
Shoots three white rabbits with the rifle
Writes to his mother about his improved health

letters.topic: His health is restored by the Maine trip

tr_quotes.text: In the evening we had a royal venison supper - a pleasant change from the ordinary routine of pork + beans.
I have got enough health to last me till next summer.

headline: Dragging the sleigh back to Island Falls
summary: The return trip is miserable: sleet and rain, wretched roads, and a horse that keeps floundering into drifts until the men unhitch it and haul the sleigh themselves. Wet, chilled and hungry after walking the whole way, Roosevelt still notes snow buntings singing, and reaches Island Falls by teatime.

events.detail: Returns by sleigh from the logging camp to Island Falls
Hears snow buntings singing

tr_quotes.text: Several times when the horse floundered off the track into the deep snow drifts we had to unharness him and drag the sleigh ourselves for a hundred yards or so.

headline: A raccoon and a camp on Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: After another empty seven-mile trap round, Roosevelt follows a raccoon's track and shoots it from a dead tree. The party then snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps at its foot, picking up two spruce grouse on the way in the best snow conditions of his stay.

events.detail: Tracks and shoots a raccoon
Snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps
Shoots two spruce grouse in a swamp

tr_quotes.text: The snowshoing, for the first time since I have been up here, was capital.

uncertain: The record spells the lake 'Mattawomkeag'.

headline: Long-range rifle practice on the ice
summary: The party breaks camp and returns to Island Falls by dinner, traveling over the frozen lake and river. Seeing no game, they pass the time shooting at targets 300 to 500 yards off, and all three do well with a Sharps rifle.

events.detail: Returns to Island Falls over the frozen lake and river
Target shooting at 300 to 500 yards with a Sharps rifle

tr_quotes.text: I enjoyed the walk extremely.

headline: Counting trophies from two happy weeks
summary: A last morning hunt turns up no partridges and empty traps, but Roosevelt is content. He sums up the trip as his pleasantest two weeks ever, with skins of fox, lynx, raccoon and buck to take home, plenty of game eaten and many specimens collected.

events.detail: Final partridge hunt and trap round, both empty
Takes stock of skins and specimens collected

tr_quotes.text: However I have had good success this trip, and I have never passed a pleasanter two weeks. The skins of the fox, lucivee [lynx], coon and buck make quite a set of trophies;

uncertain: The record also quotes Bill Sewall's later memory of TR on this trip, taken from Morris; it is not repeated here.

headline: Leaving Maine to catch up on studies
summary: Roosevelt leaves by sleigh at five in the morning for Mattawamkeag and boards the night train to Boston. He resolves to work double time until Easter to make up for the holiday.

events.detail: Sleigh ride to Mattawamkeag at dawn
Night train toward Boston

tr_quotes.text: I am now going to study all the time till Easter, doing double work to make up for my holiday.

headline: Back at Harvard, too late for church
summary: After a train held up six hours, Roosevelt reaches Cambridge late Sunday morning and writes his mother from the Porcellian Club that he arrived too late for church.

events.detail: Reaches Cambridge after a six-hour train delay
Writes his mother from the Porcellian Club

letters.topic: His late arrival back at Cambridge

tr_quotes.text: Got home this morning at 11 o'clock, too late for church.

headline: Boxing for the lightweight cup
summary: Roosevelt boxes in the Harvard lightweight competition, beating W. W. Coolidge before losing to the champion, C. S. Hanks. He weighs in at 135 pounds. He also notes he has nearly caught up on the work missed in Maine. Owen Wister later made this bout famous.

events.detail: Defeats W. W. Coolidge in the lightweight sparring contest
Loses to the champion, C. S. Hanks
Studies hard to recover time lost on the Maine trip

tr_quotes.text: Sparred for the light weight cup; won against my first man but was beaten by Hanks, the champion.
have been studying extremely hard the past week and have succeeded in making up pretty much all I lost while I was in Maine.

references.title: Roosevelt: The Story of a Friendship

uncertain: A page reference to Morris is hard to read in the record and is read as pages 112-113. Hanks's initials are also unclear.

headline: Telling Conie about the bout
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne that he placed second in the sparring contest and had a fine time in Maine.

events.detail: Letter to Corinne about boxing and the Maine trip

letters.topic: Second place in boxing; enjoyment of the Maine trip

tr_quotes.text: 2nd best in sparring contest

summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Overnight with the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt goes out to Chestnut Hill to dine and sleep at the Saltonstalls', who make him feel like family. He spends the evening at the Lees' with Alice Lee and plans to give Alice and Rose Saltonstall rugs made from his Maine fox and lynx skins.

events.detail: Dines and stays the night with the Saltonstall family
Evening at the Lee home with Alice

tr_quotes.text: They were so cordial and so glad to see me that I felt exactly as if I were at home.
I passed the evening at the Lees, with pretty Alice.

headline: D.K.E. theatricals
summary: Roosevelt takes in the Delta Kappa Epsilon club's theatricals, which he rates as very good, followed by a convivial night.

events.detail: Attends the D.K.E. theatricals

tr_quotes.text: D.K.E. theatricals. They were very good

headline: Hasty Pudding show and a gift of poems
summary: Roosevelt calls the Hasty Pudding theatricals the best he has seen, and enjoys the singing that follows in the club room and the Yard. He mails his sister Corinne a little volume of verse, Charles Fletcher Lummis's Birch Bark Poems.

events.detail: Attends the Hasty Pudding theatricals and singing
Sends Corinne a copy of Birch Bark Poems

letters.topic: Sends her a small book of poetry by Lummis

tr_quotes.text: Pudding Theatricals. They were excellent - I have never seen better.

headline: Skipping supper to see Alice
summary: Roosevelt ducks out of the start of a Porcellian supper to join Jack Tebbetts' party with Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and other young women, then returns around eleven for the rowdy end of the club evening, where a tipsy Otho Williams asks him to be his second in a mock duel with Charley Sprague.

events.detail: Visits Jack Tebbetts' party to see Alice Lee and friends
Returns for the Porcellian supper

tr_quotes.text: I enjoyed myself very much indeed.

uncertain: The Rotch sisters were also present; first names not given.

headline: Eastern photographs for Sunday school
summary: At his Sunday school class Roosevelt shows the boys a batch of photographs from the East, which makes for an unusually lively session. In the evening he calls on Jeannie Hooper and Mrs. Jude.

events.detail: Teaches Sunday school, showing photographs from the East
Evening calls on Jeannie Hooper and Mrs. Jude

tr_quotes.text: Had a very unusually interesting time at Sunday School, showing the boys a lot of eastern photographs.

headline: Private theatricals at Minot Weld's
summary: Roosevelt drives to Minot Weld's for amateur theatricals, sitting beside Alice Lee and later spending much of the evening with Nana Rotch. Back around one, he stays up singing and talking at the Porcellian until three.

events.detail: Attends private theatricals at the Weld home
Sings and talks at the Porcellian into the small hours

tr_quotes.text: I sat by pretty Alice Lee before and during the performance, and spent most of the remainder of the evening with Nana Rotch; so it is needless to say I enjoyed myself very much.

headline: Game supper at the Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt shares a game supper at the Porcellian Club with Otho Williams, Jim Wright and Charley Sprague.

events.detail: Game supper with club friends

tr_quotes.text: Otho Williams, Jim Wright, Charley Sprague and myself had a very pleasant game supper in the Porc.

headline: A lunch party and gifts of fur rugs
summary: Roosevelt hosts a luncheon in his rooms, with Mrs. Saltonstall as chaperone, for Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and a dozen friends, then shows them the Porcellian and Pudding clubs. He gives Alice the lynx rug and Rose the fox; Alice is making him slippers. That night he sails for New York with Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall.

events.detail: Hosts a lunch party in his college rooms
Presents fur rugs from his Maine hunt to Alice and Rose
Night boat to New York with Weld and Saltonstall

tr_quotes.text: I gave Alice the lynx skin, made into a rug; and Rose the fox. Alice is making me a pair of slippers.

uncertain: 'Gordy Lane' given as Gordon Lane; 'Ell. Whitney' left as written.

headline: Shaving off the whiskers
summary: Home in New York for vacation, Roosevelt shows Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall the city. At Aunt Annie's that evening he sees Fanny Smith, Margie Tuckerman and Edith Carow. He announces to his sister Corinne that his side-whiskers are gone.

events.detail: Shows his college friends around New York
Evening at Aunt Annie's with Edith Carow and friends
Writes Corinne that he has shaved his whiskers

letters.topic: Announces that he has shaved off his whiskers

tr_quotes.text: Edith is just the same sweet little flirt as ever.
Pet Pussie: At last the deed is done and I have shaved off my whiskers!

headline: Worry over a sick mother
summary: Christine and Lucy Kean come to lunch, and Roosevelt likes them both. His mother has fallen ill, which leaves him feeling wretched.

events.detail: Lunch with Christine and Lucy Kean
His mother is sick

tr_quotes.text: Darling little Muffie has gotten sick; and it makes me feel miserable.

uncertain: 'Muffie' read as TR's pet name for his mother, consistent with 'Motherling' on April 8.

headline: Elliott's dinner at the Jockey Club
summary: Elliott hosts a dinner at the Jockey Club. Roosevelt travels in Harold Haddon's dog cart while the rest of the party, including Grove Porter and Ike Iselin, comes by drag, and he takes a strong liking to Haddon.

events.detail: Dinner at the Jockey Club given by Elliott

tr_quotes.text: We enjoyed ourselves extremely.

headline: Consoling cousin Emlen
summary: Roosevelt's cousin Emlen has been turned down by Grace Parish, and the two have a long talk. His mother is still unwell.

events.detail: Long talk with Emlen after Grace Parish rejects him
His mother remains ill

tr_quotes.text: Poor old Em has been rejected by Grace Parish!
It is awfully hard on him.

headline: Lunch downtown, dinner at West's
summary: Emlen treats the group to a successful lunch at the Down Town Club, and they dine at cousin West's before an evening at the theater.

events.detail: Lunch at the Down Town Club hosted by Emlen
Dinner at West Roosevelt's, then the theater

tr_quotes.text: Emlen gave us a lunch in the Down Town Club

headline: Dog show, then the night train north
summary: Roosevelt visits the dog show, lunches with Lizzie Moran and escorts Annie Murray to a rehearsal for the Fancy Dress Ball before catching the night train to Boston. His guests loved the holiday, and his mother is nearly recovered.

events.detail: Visits the dog show and lunches with Lizzie Moran
Takes Annie Murray to the Fancy Dress Ball rehearsal
Night train back to Boston

tr_quotes.text: Motherling is almost well again.

headline: Back to work at Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is back in Cambridge and picks up his studies again.

events.detail: Resumes his studies after vacation

tr_quotes.text: Started work again.

summary: Roosevelt spends the afternoon at Nana Rotch's, teaching her the five-step waltz.

headline: Exams done and a horse arrives
summary: After two examinations and a week of hard study, Roosevelt welcomes his horse to Cambridge, stabling it at Pike's for the spring. He heads to Chestnut Hill for the weekend and dines at the Lees'.

events.detail: Sits two examinations during the week
His horse arrives and is boarded at Pike's Stable
Goes to Chestnut Hill for the weekend; dines at the Lees'

tr_quotes.text: My horse has arrived; I determined to keep him in Cambridge this Spring. I keep him at Pikes Stable.

headline: A snowy walk with Alice
summary: Snow falls all day at Chestnut Hill, but Roosevelt takes a long walk with Alice Lee anyway. He spends much of the day showing the young women how to dance the five-step, plus a newer step called the knickerbocker, and the evening goes to whist and ghost stories.

events.detail: Long walk in the snow with Alice
Teaches new dances; whist and ghost stories in the evening

tr_quotes.text: Snowed heavily all day long!
In the evening we played whist and read ghost stories.

headline: Church and a walk at Chestnut Hill
summary: After church the party visits the Francises, and in the afternoon Roosevelt walks out with Codman, Rose Saltonstall and Alice Lee. He writes his sister Bamie an account of the day.

events.detail: Attends church
Calls on the Francis family; afternoon walk
Describes the day in a letter to Bamie

letters.topic: His Sunday at Chestnut Hill: church and a long walk

tr_quotes.text: After Church we went to the Francises.

headline: First ride on the new horse
summary: Roosevelt returns reluctantly to Cambridge after two days of rest. That afternoon he rides his horse for the first time; it goes well and is full of spirit, which he enjoys.

events.detail: Returns to Cambridge from Chestnut Hill
First ride on his horse in Cambridge

tr_quotes.text: In the afternoon took my horse out for the first time; he went beautifully, but of course is full of the Old Harry - which adds greatly to the enjoyment.

headline: Riding and the Jeffries collections
summary: Roosevelt rides again, calling the horse the one thing missing from his happiness this spring. He visits the Jeffries family to look over their collections, stays for dinner and plays whist.

events.detail: Daily ride
Examines the Jeffries family's collections and dines there

tr_quotes.text: It was the one thing wanting for perfect enjoyment.

headline: Early study, free afternoons
summary: With spring in full swing, Roosevelt rises early to study before breakfast and keeps the rest of the day for himself, his heavy work for the year done. He loves riding out to Milton, Jamaica Plain, Forest Hills and Chestnut Hill and staying for a meal.

events.detail: Studies before breakfast
Rides the countryside around Boston

tr_quotes.text: Besides the rides through all this country round Boston are beautiful.

headline: A drive with Alice, then a conversazione
summary: Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill early and takes an afternoon drive with Alice, Rose and Endicott. After dinner he hurries back to Cambridge for a conversazione at Laughlin's, where he meets a lively Miss Longfellow.

events.detail: Afternoon drive with Rose, Alice and Endicott
Attends a conversazione at Laughlin's; meets Miss Longfellow

tr_quotes.text: a bright, clever girl.

headline: Theater in town, night at Jamaica Plain
summary: Roosevelt gallops out past Watertown to work off his horse's winter coat. He dines in Boston with Harry Chapin at Young's Hotel, catches a play with Weld and Dick Saltonstall, and goes home with Weld to Jamaica Plain for the night.

events.detail: Fast ride beyond Watertown
Dinner at Young's Hotel and the theater
Spends the night at Weld's home in Jamaica Plain

tr_quotes.text: I am trying to sweat the horses winter coat off him.

headline: A flirtation he regrets
summary: Roosevelt tours Minot Weld's livestock, then drives to Chestnut Hill, where he spends the afternoon with Nana Rotch and later wishes he had not flirted with her. At a Porcellian dinner, Van Rensselaer confides his feelings for Lulu Lane.

events.detail: Looks over Minot Weld's poultry and cattle
Afternoon at Chestnut Hill with Nana Rotch, Alice and Rose
Porcellian dinner beside Van Rensselaer

tr_quotes.text: I sincerely wish I had not
In vino veritas.

uncertain: The record spells Van Rensselaer several ways.

headline: Last Sunday school class of the year
summary: Roosevelt teaches his Sunday school class for the last time before summer, handing every boy a present and praising their good behavior.

events.detail: Last Sunday school session of the year; gives each boy a gift

tr_quotes.text: They have been very good this year.

headline: Riding to Chestnut Hill and Jamaica Plain
summary: Roosevelt rides out to Chestnut Hill and on to Jamaica Plain.

events.detail: Rides to Chestnut Hill and Jamaica Plain

tr_quotes.text: Rode over to Chestnut Hill and afterwards to Jamaica Plains.

headline: An exam and an evening at the Rotches'
summary: Roosevelt sits an hour-long exam and spends the evening with the Rotch family. He writes his mother asking her to send along some suits and hoping she is well and resting.

events.detail: One-hour examination
Evening at the Rotch home
Asks his mother to send his suits

letters.topic: Requests suits of clothes; hopes she is well

tr_quotes.text: Spent the evening at the Rotches.

headline: Theater party with Alice
summary: Roosevelt and Harry Shaw take Mr. and Mrs. Saltonstall, Rose and Alice to the theater after dining together. He and Alice sit a row behind the others.

events.detail: Co-hosts a theater party with Harry Shaw

tr_quotes.text: Alice and I sat just behind the others

headline: Calling on the Welds
summary: Roosevelt rides to Jamaica Plain to pay a call on the Weld family.

events.detail: Rides to Jamaica Plain to visit the Welds

tr_quotes.text: Rode over to the Jamaica Plains to call on the Welds.

headline: A rifle match, won and lost
summary: In a shooting match Roosevelt outscores Sam Skinner but falls to Fred Sharon.

events.detail: Rifle match: beats Sam Skinner, loses to Fred Sharon

tr_quotes.text: Had a rifle match beating Sam Skinner and being beaten by Fred Sharon.

headline: Lunch with the Lees, a ride with George Minot
summary: Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill for lunch at the Lees' and drives Alice and Rose into Boston to see the Rotches. George Minot arrives on horseback at four; the pair ride a long way and then go to Minot's home at Forest Hills for the night.

events.detail: Lunches at the Lees'; drives Alice and Rose to the Rotches'
Long ride with George Minot
Spends the night at Minot's house in Forest Hills

tr_quotes.text: At four o clock George Minot called for me

headline: Six hours' walk with Alice
summary: After church with the Minots, Roosevelt sees Julia Bacon home, then drives to Chestnut Hill. A walking party sets out, but he and Alice Lee drift off alone and are not back until nearly six. He takes tea at the Lees' and rides to Cambridge late.

Walks Julia Bacon home
Long walk alone with Alice Lee

tr_quotes.text: Alice and I soon seperated from the others and we did not return till nearly six.

headline: Weekend news for Corinne
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne about his weekend at Forest Hills and Chestnut Hill.

letters.topic: His weekend at Forest Hills and Chestnut Hill

summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A ride with Rose and a D.K.E. election
summary: Roosevelt rides with Rose Saltonstall, dines at her family's home and passes the evening dancing and talking with Alice and Frank Lee. He returns past ten for the D.K.E. meeting, which names Woodbury Kane and Charles Dickey first and second of the class of '82's first ten.

events.detail: Rides out with Rose Saltonstall
Dinner at the Saltonstalls' with Alice and Frank Lee
Attends the D.K.E. meeting

tr_quotes.text: Woodbury Kane is 1st man of the 1st ten from '82; Charles Dickey 2d.

headline: A long day at the Whitneys' in Milton
summary: Roosevelt rides to Milton right after breakfast, stopping briefly at Chestnut Hill. At the Whitneys' he spends six hours before a late dinner rambling the woods and farm with Bessie Whitney, then rides home at dusk in high spirits.

events.detail: Rides to Milton by way of Chestnut Hill
Walks the Whitney woods and farm with Bessie Whitney

tr_quotes.text: What a royally good time I am having. I can't conceive of a fellow possibly enjoying himself more.

headline: Lawn tennis at the Bacons'
summary: Dining at the Bacons', Roosevelt is surprised to find Rose and Alice there, and they spend the afternoon at lawn tennis. He likes Julia Bacon, and rides back in time for tea at the Tudors'.

events.detail: Dines at the Bacons' and plays lawn tennis
Tea with the Tudor family

tr_quotes.text: I like Miss Julia very much.

headline: Photographs and a bicycle meet
summary: Roosevelt meets Rose and Alice in Boston, where the three sit for photographs, then goes with them to Chestnut Hill for the weekend. They watch the Suffolk Club's bicycle meet among many friends, dance in the evening, and he walks out with Alice after tea.

events.detail: Has photographs taken with Rose and Alice
Attends a Suffolk Club bicycle meet
Dancing and an evening walk with Alice

tr_quotes.text: we had our photographs taken.

headline: Church, a drive and a call on the Lowells
summary: Roosevelt again walks with Alice after church at Chestnut Hill. The group goes for a drive in the afternoon and in the evening visits the Lowells, who have a houseful of young people.

events.detail: Attends church
Walk with Alice, an afternoon drive, and an evening at the Lowells'

tr_quotes.text: After Church again went out walking with sweet, pretty Alice.

headline: His longest ride yet
summary: Roosevelt takes his longest ride so far, through the country beyond Waverley, and spends the evening at the O.K. society. His horse, now in summer coat, looks splendid; bringing it to Cambridge, he says, was his best move. He also writes to his mother.

events.detail: Long ride through the country past Waverley
Evening at the O.K. society
Letter to his mother

tr_quotes.text: It was the best stroke I ever made, getting him on here.

headline: A fall in the dark
summary: Roosevelt rides hard to and from an evening at the Lees'. Coming home at about a quarter past ten in pitch darkness, he and the horse go down while galloping downhill, a spill he admits he fully earned.

events.detail: Evening at the Lee home
Takes a fall while galloping downhill in the dark

tr_quotes.text: I rode like Jehu, both coming and going, and as it was pitch dark when I returned (about 10.15) we fell, while galloping down hill - a misadventure which I thoroughly deserve for being a fool.

headline: A lame horse and regrets
summary: His horse is lame after the previous night's gallop, so Roosevelt has to skip dinner at the Saltonstalls'. He spends the evening at the D.K.E., scolding himself for pushing the animal too hard.

events.detail: Horse lamed; cancels dinner at the Saltonstalls'
Evening at the D.K.E.

tr_quotes.text: I have been an awful fool to ride the horse so hard.

headline: Class races, then a weekend in Milton
summary: Roosevelt watches the class boat races in the morning, in the company of the Lee family. Later he heads to Milton for a Sunday stay with the Whitneys, where the evening is given to singing and dancing.

headline: Through the Blue Hills to Punkapoag
summary: The Whitney party drives through the Blue Hills to Lake Punkapoag, and Roosevelt finds the springtime country perfect. In the afternoon he walks a long way through the woods with Bessie Whitney.

events.detail: Drive through the Blue Hills to Lake Punkapoag
Long woodland walk with Bessie Whitney

headline: Charms for the girls; a horse laid up
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive a buggy to Chestnut Hill, where he presents the young women with gold and silver charms. He fears his horse is lamed for good but is glad of the three and a half weeks of riding he had. He urges Corinne to come up for Class Day.

Invites Corinne to Cambridge for Class Day

headline: The photographs are a hit
summary: Roosevelt dines at the Lees' and walks with Alice in the evening. The photographs taken earlier in the month have turned out well. John Tebbetts walks back to Cambridge with him.

headline: Looking after a drunken clubmate

At the club dinner that night, Charley Morgan, on a weeklong binge, nearly goes into delirium tremens; Roosevelt sleeps in his room and, heading home next morning in evening clothes, almost collides with a proctor.

headline: A life of luxurious ease
summary: With exams behind him, Roosevelt describes his routine: breakfast at the club around ten, his horse waiting at the door, a ride out to lunch with friends, and if not dining out, a champagne supper at the club. Pleasant, he admits, but probably not healthy for long.

headline: Junior year comes to an end
summary: Roosevelt says goodbye to the Whitneys and heads to New York. Looking back on the year, he credits his studies, the club, his horse and above all the young women of Chestnut Hill, and doubts he will ever enjoy himself as much again.

headline: Home to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt goes out to Oyster Bay, overjoyed to see his family; his mother and his two sisters welcome him warmly. Weekend guests include Russell, Haddon, Betts, Maud Elliott and the Kane sisters, and all the Roosevelt cousins are on hand.

Weekend houseguests

headline: Back to the old Oyster Bay life
summary: Roosevelt fixes up his rowboat, builds a boathouse, rows to Plum Point and sails with Uncle Jimmie, who is summering there with Aunt Annie. He relishes the outdoor life of horse, gun and boat. Edith Carow's aunt dies this day, and the Carows move to East 36th Street.

events.detail: Readies his rowboat and rows to Plum Point

tr_quotes.text: I lead just the same active, out of door life that I always enjoy so much, - with my horse, gun and row boat.
